extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of elementary (Euclidean) geometry; school and college instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for presenting, constructing, proving, and teaching the first six books of Euclid: definitions, postulates, axioms, proposition format, constructions (straight line and circle), and examination/exercise practice for learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate i — draw a straight line between any two points
rubrics_metrics.description: A right line may be drawn from any one point to any other point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid postulates the drawing of a straight line between two given points as a basic allowed construction (foundation for finite straight-line constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate ii — extend a terminated straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminated right line may be produced to any length in a right line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite straight lines may be produced indefinitely; this postulate justifies extending constructed lines as needed in constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate iii — describe a circle from any centre with any radius
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle may be described from any centre, and with any distance from that centre as radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclidean constructions are permitted to draw circles with any given centre and radius; combined with the first two postulates this gives the compass-and-straightedge constructive power (but mechanical use of rule/compass is disclaimed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom i — equality transitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Things which are equal to the same, or to equals, are equal to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a self-evident common notion; used repeatedly to equate lengths or magnitudes that are each equal to a third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ii — equals added to equals are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: If equals be added to equals the sums will be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic arithmetic/metric principle used in argument about magnitudes, lengths; used in constructions and demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom iii — equals subtracted from equals give equals
rubrics_metrics.description: If equals be taken from equals the remainders will be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when comparing remainders of equal magnitudes after subtraction-like arguments in geometric proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom iv — adding equals to unequals yields unequals
rubrics_metrics.description: If equals be added to unequals the sums will be unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to preserve inequality relations under addition of equal quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom v — subtracting equals from unequals yields unequals
rubrics_metrics.description: If equals be taken from unequals the remainders will be unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous inequality-preservation under subtraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom vi — doubles of equals are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: The doubles of equal magnitudes are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in scaling arguments and proportion reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom vii — halves of equals are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: The halves of equal magnitudes are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used symmetrically with Axiom vi in division/scaling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom viii — superposition equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes that can be made to coincide are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the geometric notion of equality by (mental) superposition — transferring one figure onto another to show coincidence; underlies the notion of congruence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ix / xi′ — whole greater than part / whole equals sum of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole is greater than its part. (Followed by fuller statement: The whole is equal to the sum of all its parts.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue inequalities (a whole exceeds any proper part) and to reason about decomposition/aggregation of magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom x — two straight lines cannot enclose a space
rubrics_metrics.description: Two right lines cannot enclose a space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: if two straight lines have two points common they coincide in direction; used to deduce line coincidence from shared points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom xi — all right angles equal
rubrics_metrics.description: All right angles are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to transfer and compare right angles by superposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom xii — parallel/meeting axiom (interior angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two right lines meet a third line so as to make the sum of the two interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, these lines being produced shall meet at some finite distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic axiom about lines meeting when interior angles sum to less than two right angles (parallels/Euclid's fifth-related behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definitions of primitives (point, line, plane, circle, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions set out exact meanings for 'point', 'line', 'plane', 'angle', 'triangle', 'polygon', 'circle', 'radius', 'diameter', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes rigorous, canonical definitions as the foundation of arguments; correct use of these definitions is expected in constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed construction operations (straight line & circle only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions in the Elements are founded only on drawing right lines and describing circles (Euclid's postulates); the author explicitly notes Euclid's aim was theoretical, not mechanical, and disclaims allowing mechanical use of ruler and compass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructions must be justified by postulates; do not assume extra mechanical tools or operations beyond the postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition formatting: combined general and particular enunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: The general and the particular enunciation of every Proposition are given in one: omitting letters in parentheses gives the general enunciation; reading them gives the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions are printed in larger type with bracketed Roman numerals, and references to other propositions use the bracketed Roman form (e.g., [III.xxxii]). This formatting rule guides both authoring and referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of a proposition/problem (enunciation, solution, demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Theorem has hypothesis and conclusion. A Problem's enunciation consists of 'data' (given) and 'quaesita' (required); 'Solution' is the construction; 'Demonstration' is the proof (for theorems) or proof that the construction meets the quaesitum (for problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and students should separate and label these parts; proofs and constructions must establish the required relation to the data and quaesita explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corollaries, lemmas, converse & contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary = deduction from a proposition; Lemma = auxiliary proposition; converse and contrapositive are identified and used (e.g., contrapositive of a theorem may be used in place of reductio ad absurdum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages explicit identification of derived results and use of contrapositive proofs where advantageous; alternative proofs are to be presented when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superposition and congruence as methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Superposition (mental transfer of a figure) is used to show coincidence and thus equality/congruence; congruent figures are those that can be made to coincide by superposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superposition is accepted as a legitimate (mental) method for establishing equality of figures and corresponding parts; its use is frequent in triangle-congruence arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and symbol conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain symbols are prescribed: circle denoted by ⊙, triangle by △, parallelogram, ∥ for parallels, ⟂ for perpendicular, ≡ for congruence; algebraic signs +, − etc. also used. Propositions in larger type; annotations in smaller type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and students should adhere to these typographical/notation conventions for clarity; references use bracketed Roman numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: When figures are not drawn the student should construct them
rubrics_metrics.description: In the following work, when figures are not drawn, the student should construct them from the given directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must be able to produce the missing diagram implied by a proposition or construction — drawing the figure is part of the exercise and proof-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination question practice after propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: After many propositions the book supplies 'Questions for Examination' (e.g., 'What is the datum? What is the quaesitum? In what part of the construction is the third postulate quoted? Where is the first axiom quoted? What use is made of the definition of a circle?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should use these specimen examination questions throughout the work to test comprehension; they form a model for in-class or homework assessment following each proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises policy: immediate and end-of-book exercises with graded difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises in the body of each Book are intended as applications of Euclid’s Propositions and are mostly elementary; the Exercises at the end of each Book are more advanced (several taken from notable sources and some original). Over eight hundred exercises are collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use body exercises for immediate practice and end-of-book collections for advanced study or examination preparation; the editor notes the pedagogical intent and provenance of many problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical aim: combine Euclid's original with modern developments
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor intends to give Euclid 'in all its integrity' while also containing modern conceptions and developments of the portion of Geometry covered, adding annotations, alternative proofs, examination questions, and supplementary propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing or selecting material, balance faithful presentation of classical proofs with modern methods, alternative demonstrations, and exercises suitable for current teaching needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative proofs and concise demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor often gives several alternative proofs, shortens repetitive verbiage of Euclid, and introduces contrapositive arguments in place of reductio ad absurdum where advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage presenting multiple proofs and concise reasoning to illuminate different approaches; indicate alternatives in annotations for advanced students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Identity (logical principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule of Identity: 'If there is but one X and one Y, then, from the fact that X is Y, it necessarily follows that Y is X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical identity principles are to be recognized and applied in proofs where unique identification of points/objects is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and classification for angles, triangles, polygons, circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise classification: supplement, right angle, acute, obtuse, complement, concurrent lines, triangle types (scalene, isosceles, equilateral, right-angled), polygon types (quadrilateral, lozenge, square, pentagon, etc.), circle vocabulary (centre, radius, diameter, inside/outside/on circumference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students and authors must use these technical names consistently; many exercises/questions test familiarity with these definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of rigor and stepwise reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions are to be demonstrated from prior postulates, axioms, definitions, and previously proved propositions; proofs should explicitly cite the postulate/axiom/proposition used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are expected to indicate where each postulate, axiom, or definition is used in a construction or proof (the 'Questions for Examination' repeatedly query this).
